name: Adiel
title: Three men named Adiel in First Chronicles
lifespan: c. 1050–500 BC (spanning three different individuals from various periods)
summary: Adiel is a Hebrew theophoric personal name formed from 'adi (ornament) and 'El (God), with the meaning "the ornament of God". The name belongs to three different men, all mentioned in 1 Chronicles, but in widely differing historical contexts. The first was a tribal prince of Simeon who participated in a territorial expansion against the lands of Hamitic inhabitants during King Hezekiah's reign (1 Chr 4:36–41) – likely in the wake of the power vacuum that arose after the fall of the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC. The second Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, who had charge of King David's storehouses (1 Chr 27:25), a trusted administrative position in the central administration of the united kingdom. The third Adiel was the son of Jahzerah and belonged to a priestly lineage from Aaron; he is listed among priests who settled in Jerusalem, in a list that was probably used to document priestly legitimacy after returning from the Babylonian exile (1 Chr 9:12). These three men represent different aspects of Israelite society – tribal political leadership, royal administration, and holy service – but are united by a theophoric name that reflects the Israelite tradition of dedicating their children to God through naming.
roles: tribal prince of the tribe of Simeon
relatedPersons: Simon-Jacob's son with Leah, ancestor of the tribe of Simeon

keyEvents.title: Adiel among the tribal princes of Simeon
keyEvents.description: Adiel is mentioned as one of the princes of the tribe of Simeon who led an expansion into new grazing areas. During King Hezekiah's reign, these tribal princes drove out the Hamite inhabitants and settled in their land, likely due to the power vacuum that arose after Assyria destroyed the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC.

keyEvents.title: Adiel, father of Azmaveth
keyEvents.description: Another Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, who served as steward over King David's treasuries. This role testifies to a trusted position within the administrative apparatus of the united kingdom, where royal resources and properties required systematic management.

keyEvents.title: Adiel in the priestly genealogy
keyEvents.description: A third Adiel is mentioned as the son of Jahzerah in a genealogical register of Aaron's descendants—priests who settled in Jerusalem. The list was likely used to verify priestly legitimacy, especially in connection with the rebuilding of temple service after the Babylonian exile, when pure descent from Aaron was an indispensable requirement for service at the altar.

versions.summary: Adiel is a name that appears in several places in the Old Testament and refers to at least three different individuals. The most well-known Adiel was the father of Azmavet, who had charge of King David's treasuries, and another Adiel was a leader in the tribe of Simeon. The name means 'God's ornament' or 'adorned by God'.
versions.title: Ancestor and clan leader in Israel

versions.summary: Adiel is a Hebrew personal name borne by at least three different men mentioned in 1 Chronicles. The perhaps best-known Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, the official who managed King David's treasuries and storehouses (1 Chron 27:25). Another Adiel was among the tribal leaders of the tribe of Simeon who expanded their territory during the reign of King Hezekiah by driving out the Hivite inhabitants and settling in their land (1 Chron 4:36–41). A third Adiel appears in a priestly genealogy as the son of Jahzerah, among the descendants of Aaron who served in the temple (1 Chron 9:12). The name means "God's adornment" or "adorned by God" and is a theophoric name that testifies to Israelite piety tradition.

versions.summary: Adiel is a Hebrew theophoric personal name meaning 'God's adornment', and it is borne by three different men mentioned in 1 Chronicles. The first Adiel was one of the tribal leaders of the tribe of Simeon who expanded their territory by displacing the Hamitic inhabitants and settling in their land during King Hezekiah's reign (1 Chron 4:36–41). The second Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, the official responsible for King David's treasuries and storehouses (1 Chron 27:25), which attests to a trusted position in the administration of the united kingdom. The third Adiel appears in a priestly genealogy as the son of Jahzerah, among the descendants of Aaron who served in the temple (1 Chron 9:12). That the same theophoric name appears in such different contexts – tribal politics, royal administration, and priestly service – testifies to the name's popularity and the deep Israelite tradition of dedicating children to God through naming.

versions.summary: Adiel is a Hebrew theophoric personal name meaning 'God's adornment' (from 'adi – adornment and 'El – God), and it belongs to three different men mentioned in 1 Chronicles. The first Adiel was a tribal prince of the tribe of Simeon who participated in a territorial expansion against the lands of the Hamite inhabitants during King Hezekiah's reign (1 Chron 4:36–41), likely following the fall of the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC. The second Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, who managed King David's treasuries and storehouses (1 Chron 27:25) – a position that testifies to trust and administrative competence within the united kingdom. The third Adiel was the son of Jahzerah and belonged to a priestly lineage descended from Aaron; he is listed in a register of priests who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (1 Chron 9:12). Although these three men lived in different time periods and contexts – tribal politics, royal administration, and priestly service – the shared theophoric name binds them together and illustrates the deeply rooted Israelite custom of dedicating children to God through naming.

versions.summary: Adiel is a Hebrew theophoric personal name formed from 'adi (ornament) and 'El (God), with the meaning "God's ornament." The name belongs to three different men, all mentioned in 1 Chronicles, but in widely differing historical contexts. The first was a tribal prince of Simeon who participated in a territorial expansion against the lands of Hamitic inhabitants during King Hezekiah's reign (1 Chr 4:36–41) – likely in the wake of the power vacuum that arose after the fall of the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC. The second Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, who had responsibility for King David's stores and warehouses in the districts (1 Chr 27:25), a trusted administrative position within the united kingdom's structure. The third Adiel was the son of Jahzerah and belonged to a priestly lineage from Aaron; he is listed among priests who settled in Jerusalem, in a list that was probably used to document priestly legitimacy after returning from the Babylonian exile (1 Chr 9:12). These three men represent different aspects of Israelite society – tribal political leadership, royal administration, and holy service – but are united by a theophoric name that reflects the Israelite tradition of dedicating their children to God through naming.

versions.reason: [major] The profile covers three individuals from different periods: David's time (united kingdom, ca. 1000 BC), Hezekiah's time (divided kingdom, ca. 700 BC), and possibly the exile period. Choosing one era for all three is difficult, but 'divided-kingdom' does not cover all three. Since the profile represents multiple people across several eras, 'united-kingdom' would also be too narrow. However, the most prominent Adiel (the tribal chief under Hezekiah) and the priestly-line Adiel fit with 'divided-kingdom' and 'return'. Given that the profile gathers three individuals, 'divided-kingdom' can be defended as the most central period, though it is imprecise.; [minor] The Family object represents a conflation of data from two different Adiel individuals: the father 'Jahsera' belongs to the priestly Adiel (1 Chr 9:12), while the child 'Azmaveth' belongs to the Adiel who was the father of David's steward (1 Chr 27:25). Ideally, this should be clarified, but given that this is a single composite profile for three people with the same name, it is an acceptable simplification.; [minor] In 1 Chr 27:25, it is Azmaveth, son of Adiel, who is mentioned, but the Hebrew text actually has 'son of Jonathan' (ben-Yehonatan) for the one responsible for storehouses in the districts, while Azmaveth was responsible for the king's treasuries. The description should be clarified. Upon closer inspection: 1 Chr 27:25 mentions several stewards. Azmaveth ben-Adiel was responsible for the king's treasuries, while Jonathan ben-Uzziah was responsible for storehouses in the districts. The description mixes these two roles.; [minor] The summary is very good and thoroughly covers all three individuals. A small clarification: Azmaveth was responsible for the king's treasuries (not storehouses and supplies in the districts) according to 1 Chr 27:25. Storehouses in the cities/districts were Jonathan's area of responsibility.

footnotes.text: The name Adiel (עֲדִיאֵל) is composed of the Hebrew elements 'adi' (עֲדִי, 'ornament' or 'jewel') and 'El' (אֵל, 'God'), and means 'God's ornament' or 'adorned by God'. Such theophoric names – which incorporate a divine element – were very common in ancient Israel and reflect the faith and piety of the parents.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles were most likely compiled during the post-exilic period to restore tribal identity and legitimize priestly arrangements in the rebuilt temple. The fact that the name Adiel appears in three different contexts – a tribal chief, an official's father, and a priest – shows that it was a widespread name across several generations in Israelite culture.

Azmavet, the son of Adiel, had charge of the king's treasuries (1 Chron 27:25). Such administrative roles during David's reign point to an advanced bureaucratic organization. Parallels to similar administrative structures are found in contemporary Near Eastern cultures, including Egyptian and Mesopotamian empires.

In rabbinic tradition, theophoric names like Adiel were understood as expressions that the name-bearer was dedicated to God's service. The meaning 'God's ornament' was interpreted to mean that the person was called to live for God's glory – a theological idea that has parallels in later Jewish naming practices.

The expansion of the tribe of Simeon under King Hezekiah (1 Chron 4:38–41) can be understood in light of the political upheavals following the fall of the Northern Kingdom to the Assyrians in 722 BC. With the collapse of the Northern Kingdom, a power vacuum arose that gave southern tribes the opportunity to expand their territories, including into areas previously controlled by Hamathites.

The priestly genealogy in 1 Chron 9:12, where Adiel is mentioned as the son of Jahzerah, served as a means to verify priestly legitimacy. Pure descent from Aaron was an absolute requirement for serving at the altar. After the return from Babylon, such lists became crucial, and priests who could not document their lineage were excluded from service (cf. Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64).

The Hebrew male name Adiel appears exclusively in the Books of Chronicles, suggesting that the Chronicler had access to genealogical records and administrative lists that are not preserved in other biblical books. This type of source reflects a rich written tradition in ancient Israel that extended beyond narrative texts.

A parallel to the priest Adiel in 1 Chron 9:12 is found in Nehemiah 11:13, where the name 'Ahzai, son of Meshelemiah' appears in a similar list. The differences between the two lists illustrate the textual-critical challenges associated with the transmission of biblical genealogies, where name forms could vary between different manuscript traditions.
